procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 20, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 502 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Calcutta High Court issued an order in Criminal Revision No. 502 of 1966, which the Supreme Court is now setting aside. The High Court's order likely favored More, as the Supreme Court ultimately dismisses the writ petition filed by More.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of West Bengal appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and dismissed the writ petition filed by More. The Supreme Court was approached because the State of West Bengal questioned the validity of steps taken by the Chief Presidency Magistrate in accordance with a notification, which the High Court seemingly disagreed with.

directions: The order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The writ petition filed by More is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Chief Presidency Magistrate had no power to issue the warrant as it would have extra-territorial operation;

facts: The Chief Presidency Magistrate issued a warrant for the arrest of a person named More, based on prima facie evidence that he had committed offenses the Magistrate was competent to try.
The warrant was a standard domestic warrant under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Because More was not in India, the assistance of the executive government was sought to make a requisition to the authorities in Hong Kong to secure his arrest and return.
law: A warrant issued by an Indian magistrate is a legal document that is only enforceable within India and does not have inherent extra-territorial operation.
application: The Court determined that the warrant issued by the Chief Presidency Magistrate was, in its nature, a legal warrant enforceable only within India.
The Court explained that making a requisition to another country for assistance in arresting a fugitive does not invest the original domestic warrant with extra-territorial power.

The actual arrest in the foreign country is carried out through that country's own legal process, such as by issuing an independent warrant or by endorsing the Indian warrant. The arrest is made under the authority of the foreign state, not the Indian court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the warrant was valid. It did not have extra-territorial operation; it was a purely domestic warrant that served as the basis for a separate request for assistance from a foreign government, which then acted under its own legal authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Fugitive Offenders Act, having ceased to be part of the law of India, could be resorted to for obtaining extradition of fugitive offenders;

facts: In the case of The State of Madras v. C. G. Menon, individuals were arrested in Madras under warrants issued pursuant to the British Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, for extradition to the British Colony of Singapore.

The arrested individuals challenged the validity of the Act, arguing it was repugnant to the Constitution of India, which had come into effect on January 26, 1950, making India a Sovereign Democratic Republic.
law: The Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, was an Act of the British Parliament applicable to territories that were considered "British Possessions" or part of "Her Majesty's dominions."
Article 372 of the Indian Constitution provides for the continuance of existing laws after the Constitution came into force.
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to equal protection of the laws.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the entire political and legal basis for the Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, had disappeared after India became a Sovereign Democratic Republic.

The Court held that India was no longer a "British Possession," which was the fundamental premise for the Act's applicability. The political background and circumstances under which the Act was created no longer existed.

It was determined that the Act could not continue to have force under Article 372 of the Constitution because its foundational basis was gone. The Indian Parliament had not enacted any new law to incorporate or adapt the provisions of the British Act.
The Court also found that the Act was inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, specifically Article 14, and was therefore unenforceable after January 26, 1950.

The Court stated that extradition between the sovereign nations of India and the UK (or other Commonwealth countries) could now only be handled through new arrangements and appropriate domestic legislation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, ceased to be part of the law of India after the country became a Sovereign Democratic Republic. Consequently, the Act could not be resorted to for obtaining the extradition of fugitive offenders.

issue.issue_text: Whether the instructions of the Government of India for obtaining extradition are an invasion upon the authority of courts;

facts: The Government of India issued a notification setting out the procedure for a magistrate to follow when an offender is not in Indian territory and their extradition needs to be secured.
Judges in a lower court (Gupta, J., and Mukherjee, J.) believed that this notification amounted to an invasion of the authority of the courts.
law: Providing procedural advice or information to the judiciary on how to obtain the assistance of the executive branch is not considered an imposition of executive will or an invasion of judicial authority.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the lower court's view, stating that no "affront is intended by issuing the notification."

The Court characterized the notification as being "only in the nature of advice about the procedure to be followed" and clarified that it "did not in any manner seek to impose any executive will upon the Courts in matters judicial."
The Court explained that the notification was a necessary measure to devise a new process for securing fugitives after the Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, was no longer enforceable in India.
Therefore, the government was simply informing the courts of a procedure that could be followed to obtain the executive's assistance, which is required for the political act of extradition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the instructions from the Government of India were merely advisory and procedural in nature and did not constitute an invasion upon the authority of the courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Extradition Act, 1962, operates as a bar to the requisition made by the Ministry of External Affairs for the extradition of the respondent,

facts: The respondent was a fugitive offender residing in Hong Kong.
The Indian Extradition Act, 1962, was enacted, but Hong Kong was not included in its schedule of commonwealth countries.
Consequently, the formal procedures of the 1962 Act could not be used to secure the respondent's surrender.
Instead, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs made a diplomatic requisition to the Colonial Secretary of Hong Kong for the respondent's extradition.
law: Extradition is defined as a political act where one state surrenders a person to another for trial or punishment.
This can be done through a treaty or an ad hoc arrangement.
Whether an offender is handed over is determined by the domestic law of the state on which the requisition is made (in this case, Hong Kong).
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the inability to use the formal procedures of the Extradition Act, 1962, did not create a legal prohibition against seeking extradition through other means.
The government's action was a diplomatic requisition, a political act, not a legal procedure under the 1962 Act.
The Court stated that if the Indian government could persuade the authorities in Hong Kong to surrender the respondent, the process was valid.
Therefore, the fact that the 1962 Act could not be formally availed of did not operate as a bar to the government making a diplomatic request.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the Extradition Act, 1962, did not operate as a bar to the government's requisition. The Act's inapplicability to Hong Kong did not prohibit the government from using diplomatic channels to seek the respondent's surrender.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Chief Presidency Magistrate had no power to issue the warrant as it would have extra-territorial operation;
appellant_arguments: The issuance of the warrant by the Chief Presidency Magistrate was a necessary and legal domestic step to initiate the extradition process.

The warrant was not intended to be executed extra-territorially by the court itself, but was transmitted with a requisition through the executive government to seek assistance from the authorities in Hong Kong.
The procedure of issuing a domestic warrant and then having the executive government request surrender from a foreign territory is a legal and proper way to secure a fugitive offender.
respondent_arguments: The warrant issued by the Chief Presidency Magistrate was only a legal warrant enforceable within India.
The warrant had no extra-territorial operation and could not be legally enforced outside India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Fugitive Offenders Act, having ceased to be part of the law of India, could be resorted to for obtaining extradition of fugitive offenders;
appellant_arguments: The action taken was valid as it was done pursuant to a notification issued by the Government of India on May 21, 1955, which provided the legal basis for the extradition process in this case.
respondent_arguments: The Fugitive Offenders Act could no longer be used for extradition because a previous Supreme Court ruling found that the circumstances envisaged by the Act had completely changed, making it impossible to adapt the Act without significant legislative changes.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the instructions of the Government of India for obtaining extradition are an invasion upon the authority of courts;
appellant_arguments: The involvement of the executive government is a necessary and legal part of the extradition process, especially when the fugitive is in another country.

The roles are distinct: the court determines if there is a prima facie case and issues a warrant, while the executive (the State) handles the diplomatic process of making a requisition to the other state. This is a cooperative procedure, not an invasion of authority.
respondent_arguments: The actions and instructions of the executive government in the process of obtaining extradition improperly interfered with or usurped the independent authority of the judiciary.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Extradition Act, 1962, operates as a bar to the requisition made by the Ministry of External Affairs for the extradition of the respondent,
appellant_arguments: The Extradition Act, 1962, did not apply in a way that would invalidate the ongoing requisition process, which was based on prior existing arrangements or notifications.
respondent_arguments: The requisition for extradition was illegal because it was barred by the provisions of the newer Extradition Act, 1962, which superseded any previous laws or procedures under which the requisition was made.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The expression 'British Possession' in old statutes survives as an artificial mode of reference and does not imply political dependence for the purpose of the statute. Such statutes do not become inapplicable to territories merely because their political status has changed.
obiter: It is not for the Courts of India to take umbrage at expressions used in statutes of other countries and to refuse to give effect to Indian laws which govern the problems arising before them.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central finding is that the process of extradition involves a clear and proper division of functions between the judiciary and the executive. The role of the court is limited to determining if there is prima facie proof of an offence, which provides the legal basis to issue a domestic warrant. This judicial act then enables the executive branch (the State) to perform its distinct function: making a diplomatic requisition for surrender to the other country. This requisition is a political act, not a judicial one, and is not intended as an affront to the courts or an imposition of executive will. The warrant itself is not executed extra-territorially by the court; it is the domestic foundation upon which the State initiates the political process of extradition.
legal_tests_applied: The Courts of the country which make a requisition for surrender proceed upon prima facie proof of the offence.
policy_considerations: The act of extradition is founded on the broad principle that it is in the interest of civilized communities that crimes should not go unpunished, and on that account it is recognised as a part of the comity of nations that one State should assist another.
